item.title: DB uncovers drug den at DIG’s house, 84 detained
item.description:
A senior police officer was removed from his assignment at Police Headquarters on Tuesday after detectives uncovered an alleged drug-party operation at his rented-out house in the capital’s Bhatara area, detaining around 85 people and recovering several types of narcotics.
The discovery was made at a property owned by Additional Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Abdullah Al Zahir, located within Police Officers’ Housing Society‑1 near the 300‑feet road.
The Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police raided the three-storey building around midnight on Monday following information that the premises were being used for drug-related gatherings.
Investigators reported recovering crystal methamphetamine, commonly known as ice, yaba tablets, cannabis, a potent variety of cannabis known as kush, alcohol, shisha and drug-consumption paraphernalia.
Police said 26 women were among those detained.
The raid was followed by an administrative order on Tuesday transferring Additional DIG Zahir from the Maintenance and Repair branch of Police Headquarters to another assignment at headquarters, with immediate effect.
The reassignment came amid scrutiny of the property’s ownership and management, although police have not announced any criminal charge against Zahir.
According to DB officials, the property had been rented out through online accommodation platforms and was being used for gatherings involving drug consumption and DJ parties.
DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md Shafiqul Islam confirmed the operation, saying detectives from the Uttara division conducted the raid after receiving information about illegal activities at the premises.
He said the house belonged to Additional DIG Zahir but had been rented to other individuals.
“The Additional DIG had rented out the house online. The tenants used the property for drug-related activities,” Shafiqul told media.
Police said the detainees included people of different ages who had gathered at the property.
Legal proceedings against those found involved in offences were being initiated, the DB chief said.
Elias Kabir, deputy commissioner of the DB’s Uttara division, said the house was rented through Airbnb and managed by a host and a co-host.
He identified Mahbubul Alam as the co-host and confirmed that he was among those detained.
Investigators have not yet disclosed how long the alleged drug-related activities had been taking place, who organised the gatherings or whether the property’s owner had any knowledge of them.
Following the raid, Police Headquarters issued an order changing Zahir’s assignment.
The officer had been serving in the Maintenance and Repair branch.
Under the new order, he was attached to another branch at Police Headquarters, effective immediately.
The administrative action came within hours of the discovery of narcotics at the property.
However, the available official accounts do not establish that the reassignment was a disciplinary punishment or that the officer was personally involved in the alleged offences.
Police have also not disclosed whether a separate inquiry will examine the owner’s knowledge of the activities, the management of the rental property or any possible negligence.
Responding to the controversy, Additional DIG Zahir told an online news portal that the house was listed on Airbnb and another accommodation platform called Traveller.
He said the property, which has a small courtyard of approximately two kathas, was also rented for social events, including birthday celebrations and “gaye holud” ceremonies.
The officer maintained that the rental listings explicitly prohibited illegal activities, drugs and alcohol and provided for financial penalties in the event of violations.
“We have strict rules in place, which include provisions for fines should any illegal activities, drugs, or alcohol be discovered on the premises,” he said.
He also claimed that renters were repeatedly warned against violating those conditions.
Zahir questioned whether a landlord could reasonably be held responsible for crimes committed by tenants without the owner’s knowledge.
“Suppose you own a flat in Dhaka and rent it out to someone. If that person engages in criminal activity behind your back, the responsibility for that crime lies with them, not the landlord,” he said.
He argued that a property owner could take action, including blacklisting or evicting tenants, only after learning about such activities.
The DB has not said whether the alleged drug parties were organised by the same individuals or whether the property was regularly advertised for such events.
Nor have investigators established whether the property owner had any prior complaints or warnings about the premises.

item.title: A troubling silence behind two Saudi executions
item.description:
Six days after Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshis over what it described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque in Mecca, new information has raised questions about the charges, judicial proceedings and why Bangladesh was not informed of their death sentences.
A confidential consular memorandum and prisoner records reportedly show that the two were detained in August 2023 under different allegations, cybercrime in one case and adultery in the other.
Neither entry mentioned a death sentence, although Saudi authorities subsequently announced that both had been executed on October 14.
Bangladesh has now sought the court judgments, details of the proceedings and clarification of whether the defendants had an opportunity to defend themselves.
Meanwhile, the families say they were unaware of any impending executions and are demanding answers.
On October 14, the Saudi Ministry of Interior announced the executions of two people it identified as Bangladeshi nationals Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhtar.
According to the statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency, the two had been convicted of committing an “immoral act” inside a mosque in Mecca.
The ministry said security authorities arrested them, investigated the allegations and referred the case to a court.
The court sentenced them to death under “ta'zir,” a category of discretionary punishment under Islamic law, citing the seriousness of the offence and the violation of the sanctity of the place and time.
The ministry said the verdict became final after judicial approval and a royal order authorised its implementation.
However, the announcement did not identify the mosque, disclose the date of the alleged incident or provide the evidence presented at trial.
The most significant new development emerged from documents obtained and information reported by two national newspapers on Tuesday.
According to a confidential memorandum dated October 18 from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah, a Saudi prisoner list received on September 30 contained both names but recorded different offences.
Nazrul Islam, detained on August 1, 2023, was listed under Saudi Arabia's cybercrime law.
Siti Akhtar, detained the following day, was listed in connection with adultery.
The documents identified Nazrul as being held at Jeddah Correctional Facility and Siti at Jeddah Women's Prison.
Both reportedly worked as cleaners for Al Majal Company.
Crucially, the prisoner list did not disclose that either had been sentenced to death.
The consular memorandum also did not explain how the separate offences recorded in the list related to the mosque incident described in Saudi Arabia's execution announcement.
These discrepancies do not establish that the convictions were unlawful.
However, they leave the precise charges, evidence and legal basis for the executions unclear.
The latest information establishes an important distinction.
Saudi Arabia had provided Bangladesh with a prisoner list containing the two names, but the list did not mention their death sentences.
Bangladeshi officials say the mission was not notified of the sentences or the executions in advance.
The consulate's memorandum also states that it had received no requests for legal assistance from either prisoner or their families.
Bangladesh's Consul General Md Sakhawat Hossain met Saudi foreign ministry official Farid bin Saad Al Shehri in Jeddah on Monday.
He asked why the death sentences had been omitted from the prisoner list.
Bangladesh also sent another diplomatic note seeking the judgments, details of the proceedings and information about the defendants' opportunities to defend themselves.
Saudi officials reportedly said the cases had passed through the courts and that a 13-judge appellate panel had upheld the death sentences.
However, Bangladeshi officials said they had not received a satisfactory explanation for the omission of the sentences from the prisoner records.
The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah first sought information through a diplomatic note on October 15, a day after the executions.
On October 18, Bangladesh raised the matter with Saudi Ambassador Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah in Dhaka and provided a copy of the earlier communication.
The following day, officials pursued the issue in Jeddah.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir described the executions as deeply disappointing and acknowledged a lapse in information-sharing.
Bangladesh has also raised questions about consular access and the handling of the judicial proceedings.
However, the government has not formally established that Saudi Arabia violated international law.
Officials say they need the judgments and other documents before drawing conclusions.
Nazrul Islam came from Brahmanbaria and travelled to Saudi Arabia in November 2022 to work as a cleaner.
His family says he was arrested several months later and remained imprisoned for more than three years.
His mother, Rahima Begum, said he occasionally called from prison. Their last conversation reportedly took place on October 11, three days before his execution.
His father, Abdul Basir, said the family had borrowed heavily to finance Nazrul's migration.
The family disputes the allegations and wants his body returned to Bangladesh.
Siti Akhtar came from Mirzapur in Tangail. Her family says she travelled to Saudi Arabia for employment after borrowing Tk1.5 lakh.
Her father, Fazl Mia, said she had told the family that she was imprisoned following a workplace dispute.
He said she had recently spoken about the possibility of returning home within months, leaving the family bewildered by reports of her execution.
Neither family's account independently establishes what happened in the Saudi criminal proceedings.
No evidence has emerged supporting social media claims that the two were married or had travelled to Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah.
Their families told Bangladeshi journalists that they had travelled separately for employment.
Nazrul's father said his son was unmarried.
Siti's family also described her previous marriages and her decision to seek work overseas.
The claim that they were a married couple visiting Mecca for religious purposes is therefore unsupported.
Several fact-checking teams found that a graphic video circulating as footage of the two Bangladeshis' executions actually showed an unrelated execution in Saudi Arabia in 2015.
Another video claiming to show their bodies arriving in Bangladesh was also found to be unrelated.
Airport welfare officials confirmed on Tuesday that the bodies had not arrived.
The Saudi announcement confirmed the executions but did not specify their method.
Several crucial questions remain unresolved.
What precise offences were established against each defendant? Why did the prisoner list record different charges from the public announcement?
When were the death sentences imposed? Did the defendants receive legal representation and interpretation assistance?
Why were Bangladesh's diplomatic missions not informed of the sentences?
It also remains unclear when the families will receive official documentation and whether the bodies can be repatriated.
The Saudi court judgments could answer some of these questions.

item.title: Art Dhaka to bring traditional, contemporary art together in November
item.description:
Art Dhaka, a new art fair bringing traditional and contemporary artistic practices into a shared space, will hold its inaugural edition from November 6 to 10, featuring a curated fair alongside exhibitions, installations, performances and other public engagements with art.
Founded by Durjoy Rahman, Nahar Khan, Fahd Sattar and Aumia Khundkar, Art Dhaka seeks to create a platform for artists, galleries, collectors, institutions and wider audiences to engage with a diverse range of artistic practices.
The four founders bring experience spanning art, culture, business, media and creative practice. Durjoy Rahman is the Founder of Durjoy Bangladesh Foundation; Nahar Khan is the Founder of Solis, and Executive Editor of United News of Bangladesh (UNB); Fahd Sattar is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Aloki and the Co-Founder of Dhaka Makers; and Aumia Khundkar is the Managing Editor of ICE Today, ICE Business Times and is associated with Dhaka Makers.
The fair’s curatorial direction will be led by Mustafa Zaman, Zihan Karim and Najmun Nahar Keya, who will oversee the artistic vision and selection of participating artists.
Rather than focusing on a single period or style, Art Dhaka intends to present traditional, modern and contemporary works alongside one another, bringing different artistic traditions and generations into a shared setting.
The organizers aim to strengthen connections between artists and the wider art ecosystem, creating opportunities for exchange among galleries, collectors, institutions and audiences.
The fair is also intended to provide established and emerging artists with opportunities to present their work and reach new audiences.
Expanding access to art and art collecting is another key objective. The organizers aim to make art more accessible to wider audiences, encouraging more people to discover, engage with and acquire works while supporting artists.
The five-day program will extend beyond the art fair to include exhibitions, installations, performances and other forms of engagement to offer visitors a range of ways to encounter art.
Through its inaugural edition, Art Dhaka aims to establish a platform for artistic discovery, exchange and wider public engagement with Bangladesh’s diverse art practices.
Art Dhaka will run from November 6 to 10 at Aloki, Dhaka. The fair will be open to visitors from 10:00 am to 10:00 pm daily.
Further information and updates are available on Instagram at artdhaka.fair and on Facebook .

item.title: Durga Puja to end Wednesday with immersion of idols
item.description:
Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community, will end in Bangladesh on Wednesday with the immersion of idols of Goddess Durga and her children in water bodies across the country.
According to Hindu belief, the goddess Durga will return to her husband's abode at Kailash in Devaloy through immersion.
In the capital, thousands of people will throng the Buriganga River to observe the final phase of the festival -- immersion of the goddess.
Devotees will bid farewell to the mother deity and her children - Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartik and Ganesh - through the immersion of their idols, wishing Durga's return next year.
As part of the main rituals of Dashami Puja celebrations, female devotees will offer vermilion at the feet of Durga at mandaps and temples across the city, which is part of the traditional “Sindur Khela”.
The Hindu women will then put vermilion on each other, wishing for prosperity in their lives, as a tribute to the power of Goddess Durga.
Meanwhile, Maha Nabami was celebrated at puja mandaps across the country on Tuesday.
The six-day festival started on October 16 with the incarnation of Goddess Durga. This year, Maha Saptami was celebrated for seven days.
Durga Puja, the annual Hindu festival also known as Sharadiya (autumnal) Durga Utsab, is the worship of "Shakti", the divine force, embodied in goddess Durga.
It symbolises the battle between good and evil, where the dark forces eventually succumb to the divine.
This year, Durga Puja is being celebrated at 33,165 mandaps across the country.

item.title: PM: Ousted autocrat, opposition faction hatching conspiracies to create unrest
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday said the ousted autocrat and a faction of the opposition had joined hands in hatching conspiracies to destabilise the country, urging people to remain vigilant against attempts to foment unrest.
“We’ve intelligence reports that the ousted autocrat is providing money from across the border to a particular political party, which is trying to create instability here,” he said while addressing a rally at Haji Muhammad Mohsin Government High School ground in Rajshahi.
The prime minister said intelligence reports pointed to attempts to create disorder in the country. “We say: ‘We will work, we will build, Bangladesh first.’ Those who do not believe in this slogan and principle are now involved in conspiracies,” he said, referring to recent attempts to create labour unrest at several factories in different parts of the country.
Addressing the people, Tarique Rahman said the time had come for the people of Bangladesh to remain vigilant so that no one could create disorder or obstruct the process of improving the economy and changing people’s fortunes.
He said the government had taken initiatives to reopen closed mills and factories to create employment and address unemployment.
In Rajshahi district, he said, the government had brought together businesspeople and entrepreneurs and encouraged them to reopen closed industrial units. Six closed mills and factories had been reopened over the past seven months, he added.
“The core objective is to ensure that our workers do not remain unemployed and can return to work,” said the prime minister, Announcing that the government had taken initiatives to reopen around 46 more closed factories across the country between January and December next year, he said: “We want our workers to have jobs so they can earn a living and sustain themselves.”
Tarique Rahman also said the government had decided to increase the bed capacity of every upazila health complex from 50 to 100 within the next five years to make healthcare more accessible to ordinary people.
He said separate beds for children and women, along with dialysis facilities for kidney patients, would be introduced at the hospitals so that rural people would not have to travel to distant towns for routine treatment.
At the beginning of the meeting, the prime minister distributed Tk12 crore in incentives among 38,970 sugarcane farmers in the Rajshahi region. He transferred the incentive money to the farmers’ mobile accounts by pressing a button on a computer and handed over cheques to 15 farmers.
Chaired by BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, it was also addressed by Land Minister Mizanur Rahman Minu, Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, BNP Standing Committee Member Gayeshwar Chandra Roy and members of parliament from Rajshahi.
Thousands of party leaders and activists from different units of Rajshahi district attended the meeting, along with men and women from the Hindu community.
Earlier, the prime minister arrived at Shah Makhdum Airport in Rajshahi by a military aircraft at 2:50pm and proceeded directly to the meeting venue.
Before coming to Rajshahi, he visited a Durga Puja mandap at Dharmasabha Temple in Rangpur. After his engagements in Rajshahi, he left for Shah Makhdum Airport to travel to Chittagong.

item.title: Jhenaidah man dies in Latvia after alleged torture by human traffickers; nine sued
item.description:
A 45-year-old man from Jhenaidah, who was rescued in critical condition from a forest in Latvia, died in a hospital after allegedly being tortured by human traffickers who had promised to send him to Italy legally in exchange for Tk46 lakh.
Sohel Rana, son of Abul Hashem of Halidhani union under Jhenaidah Sadar upazila, died at a hospital in Daugavpils in Latvia's Latgale region on October 8, family members said.
His wife Jesmin Sultana filed a case against nine people with a tribunal dealing with the prevention and suppression of human trafficking and migrant smuggling in Jhenaidah on Monday.
The accused were identified as Shamsunnahar, 55, her husband Shahjahan Sarkar, 58, her two sons Shohagh, 35, an expatriate living in Italy and Nasir Sarkar, 32, an expatriate living in Qatar, Sohel Rana, 41, son of Abul Kalam Sarkar, Abdur Razzak, 50, son-in-law of Shahjahan, Tonny Sarkar, 32, wife of Shohagh Sarkar, Riad Dewan, 35, an expatriate living in Egypt, and Shariful Sarkar, 48, of Ramchandrapur village in Sadar upazila of the district.
According to the complaint, the accused initially took Tk26 lakh from Sohel with the promise of sending him to Italy legally and sent him to Qatar on April 6, 2025.
They assured him that he would be taken to Italy within 90 days, but he was not provided with any work, his wife alleged.
When a return ticket was later sent for him, the accused allegedly prevented him from returning home and demanded another Tk5 lakh, promising to send him to Italy through Egypt.
After receiving the money, they sent him to Egypt on August 14, 2026, according to the complaint.
On August 25, the family received a demand for Tk20 lakh through Sohel's phone. Another Tk4.5 lakh was demanded on October 9. His family sent money in five instalments in an attempt to save his life, his wife alleged.
On October 12, Latvian police informed the family through a message that Sohel had been rescued from a forest on October 7 and admitted to a hospital, where he died the following day.
Sohel's brother-in-law Ishtiaque Ahmed on Tuesday said the family had been promised legal migration to Italy.
Instead, Sohel was allegedly moved between different countries over the past one and a half years before being tortured and abandoned in a forest near the Latvia-Belarus border.
The family later learned through the Bangladesh Embassy in Poland that Latvian border guards rescued him in an ailing condition and took him to hospital, Ishtiaque said.
Local residents alleged that at least 12 people were taken to different countries by the same group, with several crores of taka reportedly collected on promises of sending them to Italy through irregular routes.
Three other men — Ripon Mia of Garamara village, Hamed Ali of Ramchandrapur village and Jagat Ali, son of the late Taizel Master — have been missing for around 12 years, according to locals.
Their families suspect that they might also have fallen victim to the alleged trafficking network, though the claims have not been independently verified.
Halidhani Union Parishad member Shahidul Islam said the group collected money from at least 15 people in Ramchandrapur and other parts of the union, promising to send them to Italy.
Some of those people are now stranded in different countries without reaching their intended destination, he added.
Halidhani Union Parishad Chairman Advocate Enamul Haque Nilu said he learned through social media that Sohel died in a Latvian hospital after being rescued from a forest, describing the incident as deeply tragic.
Contacted, Additional Superintendent of Police Sheikh Billal Hossain on Tuesday said they have yet to receive any official information from Police Headquarters or a foreign embassy about the incident.
Authorities will take necessary action if information is received, he added.

item.title: Confusion over identity of Bangladeshi woman executed in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Conflicting reports over the identity of a Bangladeshi woman executed in Saudi Arabia have raised questions about whether she was from Tangail or Bogra. Meanwhile, the family of a woman named Sweety in Tangail says she is still alive in a Saudi prison.
The family, from Nagar Chhawali village in Mahera union of Mirzapur upazila, Tangail, said the photograph published in the media does not match their daughter. They also said they spoke to her as recently as last Tuesday.
The local administration in Tangail said it had no specific information about the matter.
Sweety, the daughter of Fazal Mia, went to Saudi Arabia to support her family financially. However, questions remain over whether the Bangladeshi woman identified as Siti Akter, whose death sentence was carried out in Saudi Arabia, is the same person as Sweety Akter of Mahera village in Mirzapur.
Several media outlets identified the woman as Sweety Akter based on emigration clearance records of the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) and her national identity card information. However, conversations with her family members during an on-site visit revealed a different account.
The family claims the published photograph does not match their daughter. Sweety’s mother, however, said many people in Saudi Arabia knew her daughter as “Siti.”
Family members said they had not received any official letter or formal information from the government regarding the execution in Saudi Arabia. As a result, they remain uncertain whether the woman who was executed was their Sweety.
According to official records, Sweety Akter was born on August 11, 2001. She received emigration clearance to travel to Saudi Arabia through S Rana Trading International on February 5, 2023. Her employer there was Al Majal Al Arabi Group Company.
Recently, Saudi Arabian authorities carried out the death sentences of two Bangladeshis convicted of engaging in “immoral activities” at a mosque in Mecca. The incident sparked widespread discussion and criticism.
The family reiterated that the published photograph bears no resemblance to their daughter.
“We have neither found Sweety alive nor received her body. We have questions about the name published by Saudi authorities and the photographs circulated through various media outlets. In particular, we believe the photograph does not match Sweety’s appearance,” they said.
However, Sweety’s mother said many people in Saudi Arabia called or knew her daughter by the name “Siti.”
Local residents said Sweety went to Saudi Arabia toward the end of 2022. They said the matter should be resolved through a proper investigation.
Sweety’s father, Fazal Mia, said: “I spoke to my daughter as recently as last Tuesday. Since then, there has been no further contact. She told me she would return home after two months. Two years ago, after an argument with other female workers employed there, she was framed and sent to prison. After that, we could not find her for one year.”
“My daughter has no relationship with anyone. However, the published photograph does not match my daughter. That is why we cannot do anything. I am asking the government to bring my daughter back.”
He added: “My daughter told me, ‘There is a lawyer. He will guide me through everything.’ My daughter herself would contact the lawyer. So far, no one from Bangladesh has contacted us about this.”
Fazal Mia further said his daughter had gone to Saudi Arabia for work 3 and a half years ago.
“My daughter used to look after people who went for Hajj. My daughter is married. She has neither a husband nor any children,” he said.
Sweety’s mother, Johura Begum, said the published photograph did not resemble her daughter.
“The name matches — Sweety. That is why we cry. They have killed my Sweety. What crime did my daughter commit for them to kill her? My daughter committed no crime,” she said.
She added: “I married my daughter off. Her marriage did not last, and she did not marry again. That is why my daughter went abroad to support us. My husband still works as a manual labourer digging earth. My daughter worked there for six months. Then, after a fight among the women, the police arrested my daughter. Since then, Sweety has been in prison. We did not speak to her over the phone for one year in between. Suddenly, one day, we spoke to Sweety again. We want our daughter back.”
Mahera Union Parishad Chairman Bibhas Sarkar Nupur said he learned about the matter through the media. He said he had also heard about the incident but could not confirm whether the woman who was executed was Sweety Akter from Mahera village.
However, Sweety’s brother-in-law, Abdul Malek, told him that “Siti Akter,” who was executed in Saudi Arabia, was the Sweety from their family.
Mirzapur police station Officer-in-Charge Abdullah Al Mamun said he had no information about the matter.
Mirzapur Upazila Nirbahi Officer Zahirul Alam said: “We are looking into the matter. If Sweety’s home is in Mirzapur, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will send us a letter regarding the receipt of the body. We are also uncertain about this.”
Tangail Superintendent of Police Muhammad Shamsul Alam Sarkar said: “We will have to check with the ministry and inform you.”
Although official records and various media reports have identified the woman executed in Saudi Arabia as Sweety Akter from Mirzapur, questions remain about her identity because the family has not received any formal information and disputes the published photograph. The matter may become clearer once the relevant authorities provide official confirmation.

Seasonal celebrations cannot remain cause for national mourning
item.description:
The horrific head-on collision on the Natore-Pabna highway, which claimed at least 14 lives and left over 30 injured, is yet another grim reminder that our roads and highways remain highly susceptible to unmitigated carnage.
The culprit, as it often is, was a driver with little to no regard for rules, operating a speeding, overcrowded long-distance night coach that had an expired fitness certificate.
Once again, speeding, reckless overtaking, and unchecked vehicular rot resulted in another accident that led to mass graves.
How many times will we need to see dozens of people lose their lives before we do something about this culture of impunity and disregard?
Data from monitoring agencies shows that every month, there are at least 4,000 deaths as a result of fatal accidents on our roads and highways. Unlicensed and unfit commercial vehicles, driven by drivers who are not fit to be behind the wheel, and owners with little to no regard for the lives of everyday people, continue to operate and put millions of commuters at risk.
With Durga Puja holidays ongoing, this tragedy carries an even more heartbreak. Festive seasons across Bangladesh trigger massive surges in highway travel as thousands of families journey home to unite with loved ones.
Yet, instead of receiving heightened vigilance, strict speed monitoring, and preventative security, holiday travelers are routinely subjected to over-speeding buses, exhausted drivers, and a total absence of traffic accountability.
It is no wonder then that as holiday traffic peaks, so do fatalities on our highways. Post-disaster condolences mean nothing to grieving families who continue to lose loved ones to accidents that never should have occurred.
Suffice to say, we need a change. Unfit vehicles and reckless drivers have no place on our roads, nor do transport owners who cannot recognize that lives are worth more than profit. Seasonal celebrations must not be continually transformed into national mourning. Enough is enough.

item.title: We cannot ignore our real wage crisis
item.description:
We should be deeply concerned by the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for 56 consecutive months, as per reports from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS).
This streak of stagnant earnings falling behind soaring commodity prices can no longer be seen as a temporary metric of market friction and must be called what it is, and what it has been for some time - a full-blown livelihood crisis eroding the very fabric of our working and middle classes.
What must be recognized is the human toll behind these metrics, which is extremely stark. National survey data from BBS shows that to bridge the current shortfall, a staggering 47.42% of Bangladeshi households - and over 51% in rural areas - are needing to take on high-interest informal debt simply to put food on the table.
When citizens are forced to borrow money not to build assets, but to cover daily meals and basic utilities, we can conclude that the state’s socio-economic safety net has effectively failed. Given that this has been ongoing for almost five years now, this failure must be attributed to every single administration we have had during this time period.
In the absence of enforceable wage protections and automatic inflation-adjusted pay revisions, workers and employees alike are forced to absorb the full, brutal impact of macroeconomic shocks while corporate margins and profits remain shielded.
We cannot have a government that continues to remain a passive spectator to this erosion of basic purchasing power. Economic progress that enriches a privileged few while draining the savings of the working majority is morally indefensible, structurally unsustainable, and not the kind of progress any nation should be proud of.
The state must act now to restore real wages before our economic squeeze fractures our society beyond repair.

item.title: Behind the white coats
item.description:
Medical college is where future doctors spend years mastering the art of saving lives. However, behind the intense study schedules and white coats lies a quiet mental health and behavioral crisis.
A nationwide study published in BMC Public Health reveals that nearly one in seven medical students in Bangladesh uses tobacco or other substances.
To understand the scope of this issue, our research team surveyed 1,129 medical students across 16 medical colleges in all eight divisions of Bangladesh. The findings provide important insights into the lives of our future healthcare professionals.
Overall, 13.64% of medical students reported using tobacco or other substances. Tobacco was the most commonly used product, accounting for 54.5%.
However, the study also found notable use of non-prescription & non-pharmacological use of sedatives (26%) and cough syrups containing codeine or dextromethorphan (18.8%).
Since these medications are sold over the counter, students can easily get them when they are stressed or can't sleep.
The data shows a clear upward trend throughout medical training. While only 4.9% of first-year students reported substance use, the figure climbs to 21.8% among final-year students and reaches 26% among intern doctors.
The relentless academic workload, long clinical rotations, and chronic exhaustion may become increasingly challenging as students progress through their medical training.
Key insights emerged regarding the psychosocial triggers behind substance use:
Perhaps the most alarming finding is the severe lack of institutional support. Over 35% of student users reported that no one had ever approached them to offer help with stopping.
Institutional interventions such as campus counseling or official support programs accounted for less than 0.6% of cessation efforts.
When asked why non-users refrained from substances, students cited religious values (68.3%), moral ethics (63.8%), and family reasons (39.8%) as their primary shields.
These protective factors offer valuable direction for designing prevention strategies.
Addressing this concern requires immediate, multi-tiered action:
Doctors are the backbone of our health system. Protecting their well-being during their formative training years is essential not only for their own lives, but for the quality of care they will provide to the nation.
Dr Shouvik Roy Subha is a medical doctor, public health researcher, and epidemiologist.

item.title: Why do foreign governments and lenders still want to invest in Bangladesh?
item.description:
The IMF's October World Economic Outlook forecasts 3.2% growth for Bangladesh in FY27, down from 4.3% in April, with average inflation rising to 10.9%.
A week earlier, the World Bank cut its own forecast to 3.4% and said the weakness would persist through FY28, while it expects South Asia to grow at 6.9%.
If the IMF is right, this will be the slowest growth since FY1988-89, and place Bangladesh last among the seven South Asian economies in its table.
India is projected to grow at more than twice Bangladesh's rate. Sri Lanka, which defaulted on its external debt in 2022, is projected to grow faster than Bangladesh this year, as are Pakistan and Nepal. The medium-term outlook is weaker still, as the IMF projects Bangladesh's growth to fall to 2.2% in FY28 (Figure 1).
Yet over the same months, despite the grim forecasts for growth, the news from Dhaka has been of foreign governments and multilateral lenders showing strong interest in deepening their investments in Bangladesh.
The joint declaration of Bangladesh and China in June committed the two governments to modernize Mongla Port, develop a Chinese economic and industrial zone in Chittagong, and speed up the feasibility study for the Teesta project. In August, the Chinese ambassador said these projects could attract around 30 Chinese companies investing about $500 million.
Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement with Bangladesh in February and an emergency support loan for economic resilience and energy supply in June. Its plans now go further, as senior Japanese diplomats told The Hindu last week that Tokyo wants to build an industrial value chain around the JICA-financed deep-sea port at Matarbari, linking India's seven northeastern states, Nepal, Bhutan, and Myanmar to the Bay of Bengal. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected in Tokyo at the end of October to seek Japanese financing for a Matarbari industrial, port, and commercial hub for 2026-2031.
On October 13, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation met the PM, who welcomed Dutch interest in the Teesta feasibility study. A senior US State Department adviser has said Bangladesh could soon become eligible for financing from the US international development finance corporation. South Korea expects its trade agreement with Bangladesh, still awaiting signature, to raise Korean investment.
The multilateral lenders show the same interest. Bangladesh is the largest borrower from the World Bank's International Development Association, with an exposure of $22.7bn as of March 2026. The ADB committed$2.685bn to Bangladesh in FY26. The relationship with the IMF is also intact.
The finance minister's statement on October 4 that he had cancelled the IMF program was read as an exit. In fact, the IMF confirmed in June that Bangladesh had applied for a new program, and in July, the finance minister said the two sides had agreed on its broad framework.
Little more than a week after his statement, the minister sought the support of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok. The government is leaving the program it inherited to negotiate new conditions. It is not leaving the fund.
Why would these governments and lenders want to invest in an economy that is not poised to perform?
My answer is that a market of more than 170 million people does not shrink when its growth rate does. That gives Bangladesh a bargaining position few countries with such a forecast have. The evidence from other countries supports four reasons.
Firstly , investors follow the size of a market more than its growth rate. In 2016, in the middle of a deep recession, Brazil still received about $78.9bn of foreign direct investment, nearly half of the inflows to Latin America.
The proposals for Bangladesh follow the same logic. The Invest Bangladesh pipeline is led by renewable energy and information technology, and the Chinese proposals include the Dhaka-Chittagong highway and waste-to-energy plants. These serve the domestic market.
By my own arithmetic, even 3.2% growth on an economy of about $470bn adds around $15bn of output in a year.
Secondly , governments compete for influence in large and well-placed countries. In 2015, Indonesia awarded the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail to China over Japan after China agreed to build it without an Indonesian government guarantee, while Japan had offered a loan at 0.1% interest.
Bangladesh sits in the same contest, as China, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States all seek a role in its ports, rivers, and energy.
China and the Netherlands have both offered support on the Teesta feasibility study. Japan's answer is Matarbari, and its diplomats cite the Southern Economic Corridor linking Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam as the model.
Thirdly , supply chains are moving out of China. Vietnam drew a record $25.35bn in foreign direct investment in 2024 as manufacturers diversified, helped by its trade agreements and lower labour costs.
The agreement with Japan, China's zero-tariff treatment of Bangladeshi goods, and the planned agreement with South Korea give Bangladesh a similar platform.
Fourthly , multilateral lenders do not walk away from large borrowers. In 2024, Egypt secured an IMF program of $8 billion, a World Bank package of $6 billion and EU support of €7.4bn. In Nigeria, where I also work, the World Bank approved about $9.35bn between June 2023 and May 2026, after the government removed the petrol subsidy and unified the exchange rate. In my reading, the financing in both countries was tied to reform.
However, most of this interest is still a promise, not an investment.
Ashik Chowdhury, who now chairs Invest Bangladesh, said in June that the Chinese company’s proposals had not been verified. Of the $1.3bn pipeline his agency reported in September, only a little over $400m had reached the decision or implementation stage.
UNCTAD puts total foreign direct investment into Bangladesh in 2025 at $1.8bn, and the World Bank's own commitment fell to $820m in FY26, its lowest. Interest lapses if the government does not convert it.
To secure these investments, the Ministry of Finance should conclude the new IMF program quickly, as finance ministry officials themselves describe an active program as a seal of approval that unlocks other financing.
In return, the government should accept the IMF’s conditions on raising tax revenue. Bangladesh collects only 8.3% of GDP in tax, among the lowest ratios in the world. The IMF mission discussed measures to raise that ratio as early as July, and no lender will drop the condition.
Each G2G partnership also needs a single owner in government and a published timetable, as the published accounts of the declaration with China give no cost or date for Mongla, Chittagong, or Teesta.
Invest Bangladesh should publish a quarterly tracker of every proposal and its stage. The government should also hold to the five-year tax outlook it presented to Chinese investors.
Size is the reason an economy like Bangladesh always has room to turn around. The governments and lenders now showing interest are betting on the market, not on this year's growth rate.
However, the turnaround will not happen unless the government removes the constraints the World Bank has named: Gas and electricity shortages that disrupt industry, non-performing loans that reached 33.2% in June, and weak revenue collection.
The Matarbari plan also depends on relations with India, as the Maitri Bridge over the Feni river, the link to Tripura, is not operating.
The government will keep its bargaining position only if it turns this interest into signed investment before the investors look elsewhere.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director of Innovision Consulting and Trustee at Panam Institute, an Economic Think-Tank .

Tanzid urges Bangladesh batters to take responsibility
item.description:
Bangladesh opener Tanzid Hasan Tamim has urged his teammates to take the onus and improve their awareness ahead of the game against Afghanistan, a match that is crucial for them to reach tri-nation One Day International (ODI) series final.

The Afghanistan game turned out to be a must-win match for Bangladesh following their 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in the opening match. Not only a victory would give Bangladesh an edge, but also they have to overcome a net-run-rate issue.

Due to vulnerable batting, Bangladesh failed to chase down 272, set by Zimbabwe in a batting-favourable condition. It prompted pacer Taskin Ahmed to express concern over the team's lack of consistency and game awareness earlier a day ago.

Today, ahead of the crucial Afghanistan match, Tanzid agreed with Taskin's assessment, admitting that the batters had failed to take responsibility while chasing the target.

"What he (Taskin) said is true. We could not take responsibility in our batting unit. The wicket was good enough, and I think the target was chase-able," Tanzid said in a video footage sent by the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB).

"I felt very good as long as I batted. Unfortunately, I got out. But I think we all should take responsibility."

 The opener said Bangladesh's batters need to approach challenging targets with a more positive and practical mindset, breaking them down into smaller goals rather than focusing on the overall total.

"Of course, it is a matter of mindset. If we play with small targets instead of thinking about 300 or 350, then things will be easier. This is how we have to set our mentality," he said.

"I think consistency and mindset are very important here. If these two come together, we will be able to do well in difficult situations."

Tanzid also acknowledged that Bangladesh had been outplayed by Zimbabwe, attributing the defeat primarily to his team's failure to perform to its potential rather than the opposition's superiority alone.

"We didn't play good cricket; they played better than us. That's why they won and we lost," he said.

item.title: Execution of 2 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia: What does the consulate’s letter say?
item.description:
Saudi authorities did not inform the Bangladesh Embassy or consulate in advance about the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals. Nor did they formally notify the Bangladeshi authorities after carrying out the executions.

This information was disclosed in a letter sent by the Labour Welfare Wing of the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah to the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on 18 October.

The letter stated that the executions came to light through reports in several Saudi media outlets, citing a statement issued by the country’s Ministry of Interior on 14 October.

The two Bangladeshis executed were Nazrul Islam Abdul Bashir and Sweety Akter. According to information in the Saudi Interior Ministry’s statement, as reported by Saudi media, the executions took place in the Mecca region. They were accused of engaging in immoral acts inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca, thereby violating its sanctity.

The consulate’s letter noted that Saudi authorities had not provided detailed information about the two individuals.

The letter further stated that the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah had requested information from the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs about Bangladeshis detained for various offences in prisons across western Saudi Arabia.

In response to that request, a list was received on 30 September. The names of Nazrul and Sweety appeared on the list, but it contained no information about their sentences.

According to the information received, they had been employed as cleaners at a Saudi company named Al Majal.

The list showed that Nazrul had been detained on 1 August 2023 on allegations of information technology-related offences. Sweety was detained the following day on an adultery charge. item.title: French PM to meet unions as govt prepares for more protests
item.description:
FRANCE-SOCIAL-DEMO-CURFEW

France's prime minister plans to meet unions on Wednesday to discuss security and has vowed a "massive" police deployment at protests, following riots in the past week that led to curfews and arrests.

The eurozone's second-largest economy was rocked on the weekend by some of its worst rioting in recent years, just six months before voters head to the polls to elect a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.

Sebastien Lecornu will meet with representatives from five unions on Wednesday morning to discuss "ways and means to guarantee the essential freedom to demonstrate" according to a letter sent to the organisations, which noted some were attempting to subvert the protests with "unacceptable acts."

More protests centred over rising living costs are planned on Saturday, organised by the "Yellow Vest" movement and high school students, with another called for November 5 by labour unions.

School students have not been invited to the Wednesday meeting.

Images of clashes, mobs looting stores and public buildings set ablaze last weekend prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

Facing angry lawmakers in parliament, Lecornu acknowledged that the security response had fallen short and promised a stronger approach ahead of the new wave of protests.

"The deployment for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu said.

Arrests and investigations

French authorities announced on Monday partial curfews in Paris and other cities, and Lecornu said fresh ones would be imposed on Tuesday where needed.

The nighttime curfew in the capital, from 2100 GMT Tuesday, applied to Republique square in the centre-east and Les Halles shopping district in the centre.

A ban on public gatherings was also ordered for the Champs-Elysees, near several public buildings, and at train stations.

Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, after mobs set fire to government buildings and shops last weekend.

Security forces arrested a man believed to be connected to the ultra-left over the burning down of a historic town hall in Limoges, whose destruction has become a symbol of the violence.

Authorities have faced criticism from parties across the political spectrum, with far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen describing the unrest as a "wake-up call" that exposed a "profound crisis" of authority.

Recent polling suggests Le Pen leading first-round presidential voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerging as the strongest contender for the runoff.

Lecornu has accused ultra-left radical groups of forging an "insurrectionary plan" that led to the riots.

In a sign of growing political scrutiny over the street violence, lawmakers from across France's fractured parliament agreed on Tuesday to launch a parliamentary inquiry into the unrest, including possible intelligence failures, policing tactics and the government's preparedness.

Investors have sold off French debt in recent weeks amid rising doubts about the government's ability to rein in spending.

Nearly 150 people had been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts, according to the justice minister.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered to resign on Sunday, saying police "had lost control" during the unrest. Macron rejected his resignation and Nunez was also set to attend Wednesday's meeting with union representatives.

Other European countries have seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Italy's financial centre of Milan as well as in Belgium over the weekend.

US President Donald Trump has seized on the unrest in France to amplify his anti-immigration and anti-Islam rhetoric, at a time when his Republican party is facing headwinds in upcoming midterm elections.

Trump launched into a lengthy tirade at a midterms rally Monday in Kansas, saying France was being "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists."

Several analysts have countered Trump's rhetoric, saying immigration was not a driving force in France's unrest.

item.title: PSG sink Barcelona in six-goal thriller, Liverpool and Man City win
item.description:
SOCCER-CHAMPIONS-PSG-BAR/

Paris St Germain underlined their status as European champions by beating Barcelona 4-2 in a blockbuster Champions League clash on Tuesday, while Liverpool and Manchester City also claimed victories.

Desire Doue, Lucas Hernandez, Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz scored for PSG, with Xavi Espart and Lamine Yamal twice pulling Barcelona level in the second half.

Alexis Mac Allister scored twice as Liverpool fought back from two goals down to beat Villarreal 4-3 in a thrilling encounter at Anfield.

Phil Foden scored a hat-trick to lead Manchester City to a 5-1 win over AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium, with Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki also on the scoresheet as Erling Haaland was rested.

PSG outlast Barcelona

Barcelona arrived at the Parc des Princes with a perfect record across all competitions this season, but PSG proved more clinical in a breathless contest to hand the Catalans their first defeat of the campaign.

The relentless tempo took its toll, with PSG's Ousmane Dembele, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Marquinhos, along with Barcelona's Dani Olmo, all forced off through injury.

PSG peppered the Barcelona goal in the opening five minutes, with Kvaratskhelia hitting the post, before the game settled into a rhythm.

The hosts gradually took control of midfield and went ahead after Yamal surrendered possession in his own half, allowing Doue to drive a fierce low shot into the corner.

Goalkeeper Joan Garcia produced several saves to keep Barcelona in the contest before Espart, making his first Champions League start, created and finished a superb move to equalise in the 55th minute.

Ferran Torres hit the post against his former club before Hernandez headed PSG in front from a corner in the 72nd minute, starting a burst of four goals in 14 minutes.

Lamine equalised again for Barcelona with a brilliant individual effort in the 79th minute, before Vitinha responded for PSG with a fine strike 109 seconds later.

As Hansi Flick's side searched for an equaliser, Fabian Ruiz converted an Achraf Hakimi cross at the back post to seal the victory.

The result lifted PSG onto nine points and top of the Champions League standings, ahead of Liverpool on goal difference.

Foden hits three

Foden netted a hat-trick as Man City comfortably dispatched AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium.

Anderson opened the scoring for the hosts in the 12th minute before Foden doubled the advantage in the 34th.

AEK Athens pulled a goal back through Stavros Pilios in the 52nd minute, but Cherki restored City's two-goal cushion five minutes later.

Foden added his second of the night in the 65th minute and completed his treble 11 minutes later to wrap up a dominant performance.

Haaland was an unused substitute, as City gave their leading striker a rest amid a demanding fixture schedule.

Liverpool edged Spanish side Villarreal after a stirring comeback.

The visitors stunned the home crowd when Georges Mikautadze struck in the fourth minute before Sergi Cardona doubled Villarreal's lead in the 29th.

Liverpool's fightback started with two headers as Mac Allister pulled a goal back in the 36th minute before Ronald Araujo equalised in first-half stoppage time.

Mac Allister completed the turnaround with his second goal in the 65th minute, and Florian Wirtz hammered home a fourth in the 69th to cap a rampant spell for the hosts.

Tani Oluwaseyi pulled one back for Villarreal in the 87th minute, but Liverpool survived the late pressure to secure the points.

Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez levelled in the second half to earn them a 1-1 draw with VfB Stuttgart, who took the lead through Jamie Leweling before the break. Morten Hjulmand was sent off in the 64th minute, leaving Atletico with 10 men for the closing stages.

Napoli edged Bodo/Glimt 4-3 and PSV Eindhoven held off Porto for a 1-0 win, while AS Roma cruised to a 4-0 victory over Slovan Bratislava.

Earlier, Borussia Dortmund won 2-1 against Champions League debutants Sabah, while a 90th-minute equaliser from Pavel Kacor earned Slavia Prague a point in a 2-2 draw at Fenerbahce.

item.title: Bangladesh face Afghanistan in a must-win game
item.description:
Bangladesh face an uphill task in their bid to reach the final of the tri-nation One Day International (ODI) series in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), with an in-form Afghanistan standing in their way.

Following a 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in the opening match, Bangladesh are in a must-win situation as they take on Afghanistan in their final group-stage match at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday. The match will begin at 5.30 PM, Bangladesh time.

A victory would keep Bangladesh in contention for a place in the final, but they would also need to negotiate the tricky net run-rate equation.

Net run-rate equation

Afghanistan hold a strong advantage after registering a massive 158-run victory over Zimbabwe. Their commanding net run rate means they could still qualify for the final even if they lose to Bangladesh.

Bangladesh, however, could overtake Zimbabwe in the standings on net run rate if they manage to beat Afghanistan by a substantial margin.

Afghanistan currently top the standings with a net run rate of +3.160 after winning their only match. Zimbabwe are second at -0.590, having won one and lost one, while Bangladesh sit third at -1.980 following their opening defeat.

Recent head-to-head results suggest that overcoming Afghanistan won’t be a cake-walk for Bangladesh.

The two sides have met 22 times in ODIs, with both winning 11 matches. However, Afghanistan have dominated their last six encounters, winning five. All five victories came at UAE venues in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi.

Bangladesh lost a three-match ODI series in Sharjah 2-1 in 2024. Their struggles continued in 2025, when Afghanistan swept a three-match series in Abu Dhabi, including a humiliating 200-run defeat.

In that match, played on 14 October 2025, Bangladesh were bowled out for just 93 after Afghanistan posted 293-9.

One year and six days after that heavy defeat, Bangladesh will face Afghanistan again in the ODI format, hoping to reverse their fortunes.

The two teams also played a one-off Test earlier this month, which ended in a draw despite Afghanistan being in a difficult position. The result could provide Afghanistan with an additional psychological boost ahead of the ODI encounter.

Winning the toss, however, could prove crucial for Bangladesh. The Abu Dhabi surface generally becomes slower as the match progresses, making batting under lights in the second innings increasingly difficult.

The tournament’s last two matches have underlined the challenges teams face when batting second under lights.

Bangladesh head coach Phil Simmons has emphasised the importance of batting out the full 50 overs, saying greater awareness of the match situation could have changed the outcome against Zimbabwe.

“We lacked understanding of the situation, and making sure that when we got the three wickets, we hammer down and try and get another one quickly. Although, they batted really well,” Simmons said.

“But then when we batted, we just lacked the understanding of the situation and knowing that with a start like that, we just had to make sure we bat for the 50 overs and we’d have won the game,” he added.

Bangladesh have already suffered a setback with regular captain Liton Das ruled out of the entire tournament because of a hip injury.

However, allrounder Mehidy Hasan could return to the side after missing the opening match due to fever.

item.title: Deceived into fighting for Russia, Bangladeshi families now battle debt
item.description:
Pabitra Chandra was born into an impoverished family in Gopalpur, Tangail. He worked as a carpenter and earned very little. Hoping for a better future, he sold some of his wife’s gold jewellery and borrowed money from a microfinance organisation and local moneylenders before travelling to Russia.

Although he had been promised a job, he and 29 other Bangladeshi nationals were forcibly sent to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield. His family learned from surviving companions that Pabitra had died in the fighting. Now, alongside their grief, the family faces relentless demands from creditors to repay the money they borrowed.

Pabitra Chandra’s family is not alone. The families of the 30 young Bangladeshi men who were deceived into travelling to Russia for work are facing similar hardships.

Reports indicate that 20 of the 30, including Pabitra, have died. Two others were injured and are receiving treatment at hospitals in Russia, while two have managed to return to Bangladesh. The remaining six are still being forced to fight on the battlefield.

At a press conference on 14 October, the Special Response Battalion (SRB) said that the 30 Bangladeshis had travelled to Russia on 7 May through three organisations named Jabal-e-Noor, RS International and TS Group. Each man was charged an average of Tk 1 million on the promise of employment at construction companies.

After they arrived in Russia, however, their passports and mobile phones were confiscated, and they were handed over to the Russian military instead of being given the promised jobs.

Following 21 days of military training, they were deployed to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield. Seventeen of the 30 were killed in drone strikes on the very first day. Three more died at different times afterwards.

Families in desperate circumstances

Pabitra Chandra, 30, has two daughters aged six and eight. After hearing reports of his death, his wife developed psychological problems. Sometimes she laughs, sometimes she cries.

Pabitra had travelled to Russia with Tk 130,000 raised by selling his wife’s jewellery and another Tk 950,000 borrowed from a microfinance organisation and local moneylenders.

Pabitra’s brother-in-law, Tapan Chandra Sutradhar, told Prothom Alo that the family had been in contact with him for the first few days after he arrived in Russia. At the time, Pabitra said that he and several others were staying at a hotel and would be given jobs once their paperwork was completed.

Bangladeshis sent to Russia for jobs, used as 'prey' in war, 20 killed: SRB

After contact was lost for some time, he called his family on 29 May and said, “They are forcing us to go to war. The risk of dying there is 95 per cent.”

Pabitra subsequently contacted the Bangladesh embassy and requested assistance in arranging the return of himself and the others to Bangladesh. He also apologised to his family for his mistakes.

The family later learned of his death from his companions. However, neither the embassy nor any government source has officially confirmed the news to them.

Tapan Chandra said, “The family has reached such a desperate situation that when they sit down to eat, creditors come and stand behind them demanding money. They are now considering selling the remaining three decimals of land, but even that will not be enough to repay the loans. Still, the family’s last hope is that Pabitra might be alive.”

Robin Mir used to drive an auto-rickshaw in Siddhirganj, Narayanganj. He, too, travelled to Russia in search of work after selling land and livestock in his village and taking out loans. Three other men from Narayanganj went with him. His family learned of his death through them.

Robin’s nephew, Rahat Chowdhury, told Prothom Alo that his uncle was given good food and taken sightseeing for the first three or four days after arriving in Russia. Then the family heard nothing from him for five or six days.

How middlemen recruit Bangladeshi youth for Russia-Ukraine war

On 15 May, Robin informed them that they were being taken to work. Contact was subsequently lost again. On 17 May, the family saw him in a video from a military camp.

On 29 May, Robin called his family in tears and said, “They promised us jobs, but took us through a dense forest and sold us off.”

That was the last time Rahat spoke to his uncle.

Rahat said his uncle’s wife and two children were now living in desperate circumstances. The daughter is nine years old and the son is five. Creditors call repeatedly and subject the family to verbal abuse. Sometimes, the family has enough food for one meal but nothing for the next.

In addition to Pabitra and Robin, Prothom Alo spoke to family members of seven of the 30 Bangladeshis who travelled to Russia. Almost all the families are from low-income backgrounds.

According to information provided by the families, the other 18 men reported killed on the battlefield are Sohel, Md Mehedi Hasan, Md Al Mamun, Md Abdullah Al Mamun, Md Nazmul Alam, Md Wasim Akram, Md Arif Hossain, Md Sayeed Molla, Tarikul Islam Mintu, Sabbir Hossain, Mofiz, Md Arman Ali, Md Nazrul Islam, Md Aminul Islam, Kazi Rezaul Karim, Main Uddin, Ripon Hossain and Arif Hossain Patwary.

Of the 30 Bangladeshis who were deceived, Rajon Hossain and Adnan Hossain have managed to return to Bangladesh. Palash Sheikh and Ali Hasan Sohel were injured and are receiving treatment at hospitals in Russia.

6 still on the battlefield

Roni Sheikh of Gopalganj, Al Amin Islam of Lalmonirhat, Sourav Molla of Gopalganj, Kamal Hossain of Madaripur, Abu Hanif of Kishoreganj and Helal Sheikh of Madaripur are still being forced to fight on the Russia-Ukraine battlefield. Some of them remain in contact with their families.

Taslim Sardar, the husband of Sourav Molla’s younger sister, regularly communicates with Sourav through the messaging app Imo.

Taslim told Prothom Alo that Sourav was currently stationed three to four kilometres behind the frontline. He was being made to dig earth for bunkers, and something could happen to him at any time. He had tried to escape twice but had failed.

Taslim recently joined the families of the victims in holding a human chain protest in Dhaka.

He said Kamal was working alongside Sourav, digging earth for bunkers. Roni Sheikh and Al Amin were walking from their camp to the frontline to deliver food, water and weapons. Hanif and Helal had no fixed duties. They were assigned various tasks, including digging bunker trenches and delivering food.

item.title: Bijoya Dashami Wednesday as Durga Puja concludes with idol immersion
item.description:
Sharadiya Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of the Hindu community, concludes on Wednesday with the immersion of idols on the occasion of Bijoya Dashami.
After five days of rituals and festivities, Goddess Durga is set to return to her heavenly abode at Kailash, leaving devotees with a sense of melancholy at puja mandaps across the country.
Devotees have been gathering at puja mandaps since morning to mark Bijoya Dashami. As they bid farewell to the Goddess, they are offering prayers for peace, prosperity and well-being for their families, society and the nation.
According to schedules released by the Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee and Dhakeshwari National Temple authorities, the Dashami Bihita Puja and Darpan Bisarjan, the symbolic immersion of the deity’s reflection, are scheduled to be completed by 9:57am.
The day's key rituals include Devi Baran and Sindur Khela. Before the immersion, married women bid farewell to the Goddess by applying vermilion to her and offering sweets, praying for their husbands' longevity and the happiness, well-being and prosperity of their families.
They then apply vermilion, first touched to the Goddess's feet, to one another's foreheads and cheeks. The ritual is accompanied by dance, music and the exchange of sweets. Unmarried women and other devotees also join the festivities.
According to the schedule, Devi Baran is set to begin at 11:30am, followed by a voluntary blood donation program at noon.

item.title: Intern doctors at RMCH halt work over five-point demand
item.description:
Intern doctors at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital launched a 24-hour work stoppage at 8am on Wednesday, pressing for a five-point set of demands, including addressing shortages of medical supplies and improving security.
The work stoppage has disrupted medical services at the hospital, causing hardship for patients, many of whom have travelled from distant areas, and their relatives.
The protesting doctors said essential medicines and medical supplies were in short supply in the hospital’s inpatient wards. They also complained of difficulties caused by the unrestricted entry of patients’ relatives into the wards and alleged negligence by Ansar personnel responsible for security. They further claimed to have faced organized threats.
The interns said the hospital’s observation room and casualty department were currently non-functional, increasing the pressure on inpatient wards. They said limited staffing and inadequate medical supplies had made it difficult to provide proper care.
According to the protesters, the hospital administration had repeatedly assured them that the problems would be addressed but had taken no effective steps. They said the work stoppage was a last resort.
Dr S M Tapu, president of the Intern Doctors’ Society at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital, said a press conference would be held on Wednesday afternoon to outline the demands, explain the situation and announce their next course of action.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 9th among world’s most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 9th among the world's most polluted cities on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 162 at 10:05am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Lahore in Pakistan ranked first with an AQI score of 272, while Delhi in India ranked second with a score of 249, followed by Jakarta in Indonesia third place with an AQI score of 183.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: PSG late show downs Barca in Champions League, Liverpool fight back in 7-goal thriller
item.description:
Holders Paris Saint-Germain made it three wins from three in this season's Champions League, beating Barcelona 4-2 thanks to late goals from Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz on Tuesday, while Liverpool clinched a dramatic comeback victory over Villarreal.
Phil Foden scored a hat-trick as Manchester City thrashed AEK Athens 5-1, while there were also much-needed wins for Roma and Napoli.
PSG kept their place at the top of the league-phase table, but could yet count the cost of injuries suffered by Ousmane Dembele, Marquinhos and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia at the Parc des Princes.
"We don't feel superior to any team but we trust in ourselves, in everyone who starts and who comes off the bench," Paris midfielder Ruiz told Movistar. "There's still a long way to go."
Barcelona twice levelled against the two-time defending champions, but were ultimately well beaten as they slipped to their first defeat of the season.
"We tried to play how we want to play, we pressed them very high. There were a lot of fantastic things on show today," said Flick, whose team had won their previous 11 games in all competitions this term.
Kvaratskhelia hit the post, Dembele hobbled off and Ferran Torres was denied by Barca goalkeeper Joan Garcia in a fast-paced opening.
PSG took a deserved lead in the 38th minute as Desire Doue collected the ball outside the area and thumped a shot into the bottom corner.
Garcia made another excellent save shortly after the break from Achraf Hakimi, before Xavi Espart burst through to level for Barca against the run of play.
Kvaratskhelia and Marquinhos both pulled up injured within seconds of each other and had to leave the field.
The home team continued to press, though, and Lucas Hernandez restored their advantage 18 minutes from time with a brilliant header.
Lamine Yamal powered past Warren Zaire-Emery to equalise again seven minutes later.
But Vitinha hammered home from outside the box in the 81st minute and Ruiz's tap-in gave Luis Enrique's team a second straight 4-2 Champions League win after seeing off Man City by the same scoreline last week.
Liverpool battled back from two goals down to also maintain their 100-percent record by edging out Villarreal 4-3 at Anfield.
Liverpool fell behind in the fourth minute when Georges Mikautadze pounced on a terrible error from Virgil van Dijk, before Villarreal defender Sergi Cardona strolled through their defence to make it two.
Alexis Mac Allister pulled one back for the hosts nine minutes before half-time by heading in Kostas Tsimikas's corner.
Andoni Iraola's men were level in first-half added time through Ronald Araujo's back-post header after Cardona inexplicably left Rio Ngumoha's cross.
Mac Allister completed the turnaround by firing in from Ngumoha's square pass, and half-time substitute Florian Wirtz's first goal of the season gave the Reds some breathing space.
Tani Oluwaseyi set up a nervy finish for Iraola, but Liverpool held on.
"We are facing very good teams. It's good to come back but we've started losing too many goals this season," Iraola told Amazon Prime.
At the Etihad, Elliot Anderson put Manchester City in front with his first goal for the club, before Phil Foden made it two goals in as many games after scoring against Ipswich at the weekend.
AEK halved the deficit early in the second half through Stavros Pilios, only for Rayan Cherki to sweep in City's third in the 57th minute.
Foden later fired in his second and third goals in a comprehensive victory, despite Erling Haaland being rested after picking up a knock at the weekend.
"Slowly, but surely. Still got a long way to go, but I am going in the right direction," Foden told TNT Sports of his gradual return to form.
Roma eased to their first Champions League win since 2019 as the capital club brushed aside pointless Slovan Bratislava 4-0 at the Stadio Olimpico.
All four Serie A clubs in the competition lost last week, but Napoli made it two wins from two on Tuesday for the Italian sides.
Massimiliano Allegri's men were twice pegged back by Bodo/Glimt but eventually got the better of the Norwegians in a 4-3 thriller, as Scott McTominay scored a brace.
Atletico Madrid played out a 1-1 draw with Stuttgart in Germany, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men.
Borussia Dortmund ended a run of four straight away defeats in the Champions League with a 2-1 win over Sabah in Baku.

item.title: Trump says he wants Zelensky to 'make a deal' with Russia
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday urged Volodymyr Zelensky to make a deal with Russia -- redoubling pressure on the Ukrainian leader even as Moscow grinds on with the war it launched four years ago.
Trump also said he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to release Stephen Hubbard -- an American taken captive by Moscow's forces years earlier in Ukraine -- in a fresh sign of his pivot back to Moscow.
"We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," Trump told reporters in the same room.
Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Zelensky had a bruising televised confrontation in the Oval Office in February 2025, shortly after the Ukraine-skeptic US president returned to office.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump said Tuesday.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The Ukrainian leader met Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday for talks aimed at easing the tensions.
Zelensky hailed the resumption of US intelligence sharing on looming Russian strikes, but insisted Kyiv must be included in any future talks on its fate after meetings with US envoys.
Ukraine has been increasingly alarmed by Trump's return to effectively blaming Kyiv for a failure to end the war that began with Moscow's February 2022 invasion, and by his warm words towards Putin.
Trump indicated that a deal with Russia to free Hubbard could be near.
"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said in response to a question from an AFP journalist.
"Just stick with me," Trump added. "Just you remember that question a couple of days from now, because I do things that nobody else can do."

item.title: Bangladesh elect to bat, need 41-run win over Afghanistan to reach final
item.description:
Bangladesh won the toss and elected to bat first against Afghanistan as they seek a place in the final of the tri-nation One Day International (ODI) series in the United Arab Emirates, needing a convincing victory in their final group-stage match on Wednesday.

Bangladesh have made three changes to their playing XI for this must-win match. Rishad Hossain, Nurul Hasan and Mosaddek Hossain, who featured against Zimbabwe, have been left out. Aliss Al Islam, Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Parvez Hossain come into the side.

Aliss, who made his international debut at last month’s Asian Games, is making his ODI debut today.

After suffering a 99-run defeat to Zimbabwe in their opening match, Bangladesh must beat Afghanistan at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi to keep their hopes of reaching the final alive.

Victory alone, however, is not enough. Bangladesh also need to overcome a significant net run-rate deficit to move ahead of Zimbabwe in the standings.

Net run-rate equation

Bangladesh need to win by at least 41 runs to achieve the required net run rate to qualify for the final.

Afghanistan hold a commanding position after thrashing Zimbabwe by 158 runs. Their net run rate of +3.160 puts them at the top of the standings after one match. Zimbabwe are second at -0.590, having won one match and lost one, while Bangladesh are third at -1.980 following their opening defeat.

Afghanistan could still qualify for the final even if they lose to Bangladesh, thanks to their strong net run rate. Bangladesh, meanwhile, need a convincing victory to overtake Zimbabwe and remain in contention.

Afghanistan hold recent advantage

The head-to-head record between the two sides is evenly balanced, with Bangladesh and Afghanistan having won 11 matches each in their 22 ODI meetings.

Recent results, however, favour Afghanistan. They have won five of their last six encounters with Bangladesh, with all five victories coming at UAE venues in Sharjah and Abu Dhabi.

Bangladesh will therefore need to overcome both Afghanistan’s recent dominance and the net run-rate challenge to keep their hopes of reaching the final alive.
