item.title: The ‘disease’ Shakib–Tamim cured is returning to Bangladesh’s batting
item.description:
If life were a cricket match, it would probably resemble Test cricket more than any other format. A long journey spanning five days. Sometimes there is sunshine, sometimes clouds. Sometimes the batters dominate; at other times, the bowlers are in control. Good times come, and bad times follow. Sometimes, it feels as though everything is over. Then, just when all seems lost, a new story begins.

In a way, one-day international cricket is life, too. Only a little shorter. A miniature life spanning 50 overs. There is room to make mistakes, and there is a chance to correct them. With patience, a team can recover from a collapse. But there is one condition: it must survive.

Bangladesh’s ODI journey has been an exciting struggle to survive. There was a time when batting through 50 overs was an achievement in itself. The fragility of Bangladesh’s batting often seemed more frightening than the opposition’s bowling.

Then times changed. Shakib Al Hasan, Tamim Iqbal and Mushfiqur Rahim came along. Bangladesh cricket moved beyond its childhood and into adolescence. Batting through 50 overs was no longer a surprise.

But does time always move forward? Recent statistics on Bangladesh’s ODI batting raise that very question. A problem that had largely been overcome seems to be returning: the old habit of seeing innings crumble before the allotted overs are completed.

Of course, there is no rule that a team must bat for all 50 overs to succeed in an ODI. A side can be bowled out after 40 overs and still win. If its bowlers produce a brilliant performance, even a modest total may be enough. And when chasing, winning a match in 30 overs is certainly a success.

But the equation is different for a team batting first. It has the opportunity to use all 50 overs. If it repeatedly fails to make the most of that opportunity, questions inevitably arise about the depth of its batting, its patience and its ability to build an innings.

Bangladesh’s story, therefore, can be told through one statistic: how often it has been bowled out before completing 50 overs when batting first.

The fragile batting of Bangladesh’s early years

Think back to the early days of Bangladesh cricket. Scoring 200 runs in an ODI was a relief. Reaching 250 was practically a cause for celebration. As soon as the opposition bowlers applied a little pressure, the batting line-up would collapse. It was not unusual to see one batter depart, followed by two more in quick succession.

The numbers tell the same story. Between 2000 and 2010, Bangladesh batted first in 82 ODIs. It failed to complete 50 overs in 48 of them. In other words, its innings ended before the allotted overs were completed in 58.5 per cent of those matches.

Put simply, Bangladesh’s batting could not survive the full 50 overs in nearly six out of every 10 matches.

And what about wins?

Bangladesh won only two of those 48 matches—one against Zimbabwe and the other against Kenya. By contrast, it won 18 matches in which it batted through the full 50 overs. The connection between surviving until the end of an innings and winning was already quite evident.

Of course, batting for 50 overs does not guarantee victory. The total scored, the opposition and the nature of the pitch all matter. Even so, the statistics from that period made one thing clear: if Bangladesh wanted to win, it first had to learn how to survive.

Then the times changed

In cricket, as in life, a change of generation can sometimes mark the beginning of a new era. Shakib, Tamim and Mushfiqur became the faces of that transformation in Bangladesh’s batting. The team gained experience alongside them. It learned how to build an innings, when to attack and when to protect its wickets.

It is difficult to compare the Bangladesh team of 2000–2010 with the side that emerged in the following decade.

Between 2010 and 2020, Bangladesh batted first in 83 ODIs. It failed to complete 50 overs in 28 of them, a rate of 33.7 per cent.

The rate had fallen from 58.5 per cent in the previous decade to 33.7 per cent—a drop of 24.8 percentage points. That was a substantial improvement. A team that once failed to bat out 50 overs in nearly six out of every 10 matches had reduced that figure to about three in every 10.

What better statistical evidence could there be of greater stability in the batting?

Bangladesh also won nine matches during that decade despite failing to complete 50 overs. In matches in which it batted through the full 50 overs, it won 27. In other words, Bangladesh had not only learned to spend more time at the crease; it had also begun turning that resilience into victories.

What do the golden years tell us?

When recalling the most memorable periods in Bangladesh’s ODI history, the years following 2015 stand out.

Shakib was then a world-class all-rounder. Tamim was a dependable presence at the top of the order. Mushfiqur was a major pillar of the middle order. Experience and confidence went hand in hand.

Watching Bangladesh during that period inspired at least one belief: losing two early wickets did not mean everything was over. An innings could still be rebuilt.

But do the statistics from those years tell a different story from the decade as a whole?

Between 2015 and 2020, Bangladesh batted first in 40 ODIs. It failed to complete 50 overs in 13 of them, a rate of 32.5 per cent. The figure for the entire decade was 33.7 per cent. The difference was marginal.

In other words, the improvement in Bangladesh’s batting was not confined to a few years after 2015. It remained broadly consistent throughout the 2010–2020 decade.

This was not a case of Bangladesh producing a few years of good batting and temporarily concealing its old weakness. Rather, the team demonstrated a sustained ability to bat through 50 overs over the course of the decade.

So where has that consistency gone?

New symptoms of an old disease

Bangladesh cricket is no longer where it was in its infancy. Expectations of the team in ODIs have changed, too. The aim is no longer merely to put up a fight; winning matches is now the natural expectation. More is demanded of the generation represented by Najmul Hossain and Litton Das.

Yet the statistics suggest that the team may be moving in the opposite direction.

Since 2020, Bangladesh has batted first in 51 ODIs. It failed to complete 50 overs in 18 of them, a rate of 35.3 per cent.

That is not much higher than the previous decade’s 33.7 per cent—just a difference of 1.6 percentage points. On its own, this may not be cause for serious concern. Such fluctuations are normal in cricket. But the picture becomes less reassuring when the calculation starts in 2023.

Since then, Bangladesh has batted first in 34 ODIs. It failed to complete 50 overs in 14 of them, a rate of 41.2 per cent. That means its innings ended prematurely in more than four out of every 10 matches.

Think about that.

A team that spent more than a decade demonstrating its growing ability to bat through 50 overs now appears to be drifting back towards its old weakness.

Of the 14 matches since 2023 in which Bangladesh failed to complete 50 overs, it won four. In matches where it batted through the full 50 overs, it won eight. Once again, the importance of batting through the innings is apparent.

Are two decades of progress slipping away?

Placing the four sets of statistics side by side makes the evolution of Bangladesh’s ODI batting clearer.

They offer four distinct snapshots of the team’s history. The first reflects inexperience. The second tells a story of growing maturity. The third suggests that progress may have stalled. And the fourth points to the return of an old concern.

A note of caution is necessary, however. A rising rate of innings ending before 50 overs does not automatically mean that batting quality has declined by the same proportion. Sometimes wickets fall as a team tries to score quickly. At other times, the match situation forces batters to take risks.

The strength of the opposition and the nature of the pitch can also affect the figures.

Nor would it be right to deliver a definitive verdict on a long-term decline based on statistics covering only a few years. But the questions are legitimate—and they should be asked.

Are Bangladesh’s batters once again losing the patience required to build an innings? Even when they get off to a good start, are they struggling to turn it into a substantial total? Or has a weakness emerged somewhere in the batting order that repeatedly becomes exposed under pressure?

These statistics alone cannot provide definitive answers. But there is little doubt that the questions need to be investigated.

In 50-over cricket, a good start is not enough. A team must negotiate the middle overs and preserve its resources for the finish. Sometimes it must unleash a storm; at other times, it must weather one. Much like life itself.

Bangladesh cricket once learned these lessons rather well. That is why signs of regression are all the more troubling.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh can bat for 50 overs. It is whether, after all these years, the team is beginning to forget what it learned.

Perhaps that is the greatest tragedy of a 50-over innings, much like life: finding your way, only to lose it again.

item.title: Rubio questions UN, refuses opinion on protests in India, says "this is a democracy"
item.description:
USA-RUBIO/INDIA

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday described the term “UN experts” as an “oxymoron” when asked about the United Nations' criticism of India's handling of protests, while declining to weigh in on the issue and saying that domestic political matters must be decided by the people of the country concerned.

Responding to a reporter's question about protests by opposition parties and students in India and the UN experts' allegations of a crackdown, Rubio said he would not get involved in India's internal political affairs.

“Well, the UN experts, yeah. My favourite. The UN experts, or is that an oxymoron?” Rubio remarked.

Clarifying Washington's position, he said, “No, it's a domestic political matter. I mean, I am not going to get involved in their politics. This is a democracy. They have elections here. So I am not going to align on their domestic political matters.”

Rubio said demonstrations and the expression of differing political opinions were part of democratic discourse, distinguishing peaceful protests from riots involving vandalism, arson and destruction of property.

He said the ability of people to express themselves and engage in political debate was an important feature of democratic societies. Citing Cuba as a contrast, Rubio pointed to restrictions faced by opposition voices there, including the risk of imprisonment, oppression or exile.

“But we're not going to comment on internal political matters. That's for the Indian people to decide and navigate,” he said.

Earlier, India exposed the double standards of the United Nations and its frontal organisations have been exposed after contrasting stands taken by the representatives to paint protests in India as an issue of alleged human rights abuse. At the United Nations India stressed that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective targeting of countries.

Indian diplomat Barkha Tamrakar who addressed the Assembly on Tuesday (local time) said that India's constitutional safeguards, including Article 21 of the Constitution, protect human rights and ensure due process, as United Nations experts raised concerns over alleged excessive use of force against protesters and restrictions on peaceful demonstrations.Barkha Tamrakar stressed that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective targeting of countries.

"India firmly opposes any attempt to convert unverified allegations, incomplete statistics, or a report that contains no India country observation into a negative characterization of the world's largest democracy...Human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective country targeting,” Tamrakar said, emphasising the need for impartial and evidence-based engagement on human rights issues.

The strong rebuttal came after UN experts had claimed that authorities in India were restricting peaceful assembly and indulging in 'enforced disappearances'. Contrastingly a much milder stand was expressed by UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk when it came to speaking of the police crackdown on violent protests in France and other parts of Europe. Turk even went to the extent of calling protestors 'vandals'.

India has strongly opposed characterisations based on unverified allegations, incomplete statistics or reports lacking India-specific observations.

item.title: Bijoya Dashami being celebrated with traditional Sindur Khela at mandaps
item.description:
Bijoya Dashami, the final day of the six-day Sharadiya Durga Puja, is being celebrated across the country today, Wednesday, with due religious fervour, traditional rituals and communal harmony.

The celebrations are drawing to a close with the observance of Sindur Khela during the day, followed by the immersion (Bisarjan) of Durga idols in nearby rivers, ponds and other water bodies this evening.

Devotees are also exchanging Bijoya greetings, marking the departure of Goddess Durga from her earthly abode.

Temples across the country, including Dhakeshwari National Temple, Ramna Kali Mandir, Siddheshwari Kalimandir and Ramakrishna Mission and Math, are witnessing large gatherings of worshippers.

Married Hindu women, dressed in traditional white sarees with red borders, are participating in Sindur Khela, one of the most prominent rituals of Bijoya Dashami.

Sindur Khela, meaning the playing with vermilion, is a traditional Hindu ritual observed mainly in Bangladesh and eastern India.

During the ritual, married women offer vermilion and sweets to Goddess Durga following the completion of the final Dashami puja. They then smear vermilion on each other’s foreheads and faces, exchange sweets and pray for marital happiness and prosperity.

Although traditionally observed by women, the ritual has increasingly seen the participation of male devotees in recent years, adding to the festive atmosphere.

Dashami puja was performed at temples and temporary mandaps in the morning, followed by Darpan Bisarjan, a symbolic ritual in which the reflection of the Goddess is immersed before the formal immersion of the idol.

Following the rituals, colourful processions are making their way through city streets towards nearby water bodies for the immersion of the idols.

The idols, traditionally carried on bamboo structures, are now being transported on decorated trucks and pickups, with some taken by boat to the middle of rivers for immersion.

Devotees are chanting traditional slogans such as “Aschhe bochhor abar hobe” (It will happen again next year), expressing their hope for the Goddess’s return next year.

In Dhaka, major mandaps at Dhakeshwari National Temple, Ramakrishna Mission and Math, Kalabagan, Banani, Shakhari Bazar and Ramna Kali Mandir have drawn thousands of devotees since morning.

The immersion ceremonies in the capital are expected to draw large crowds, while law enforcement agencies are maintaining security and taking measures to ensure smooth traffic movement.

Similar celebrations are taking place in major divisional cities, including Chattogram, Rajshahi, Khulna, Sylhet and Barishal, as well as district towns such as Narayanganj, Faridpur, Dinajpur, Jashore, Kushtia, Netrakona, Tangail and Satkhira.

Following the immersion, younger family members seek blessings from elders by touching their feet, while relatives and friends exchange warm embraces and Bijoya greetings.

Traditional sweets, including chomchom, kalojam, sandesh and narkeler naru (coconut and jaggery balls), are being distributed among family members, friends and neighbours as part of the Bijoya celebrations.

item.title: Russia to send first diesel cargo of 40,000 tonnes to US on Thursday
item.description:
RUSSIA-ENERGY

Russia will dispatch its first tanker with diesel for the United States on Thursday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said, according to the Vedomosti news outlet, after a deal with US President Donald Trump.

Russia lifted its self-imposed ban on diesel exports on 9 October, introduced to tackle domestic shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries, after reaching the deal with Trump to supply diesel to global markets.

Novak said on Wednesday the vessel will carry 40,000 metric tons of the fuel, adding that the paperwork on the fuel supply is nearing its completion, according to media reports. He did not name the port from which the cargo will be delivered.

"Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities," RIA news agency quoted Novak as saying.

Trump has said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin was hosting US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday, after the US-Russia diesel export deal led to a sharp deterioration in ties between the United States and Ukraine.

During the talks in St Petersburg, Witkoff thanked Putin for lifting the export restrictions. Putin also mentioned the deal, saying that diesel prices dropped after the agreement.

item.title: 3 tourists die while bathing at Himchhari beach in Cox’s Bazar, 2 missing
item.description:
Three tourists have died while swimming at Himchhari beach in Cox's Bazar and two others are missing today, Wednesday, around 4: 30 PM at the beach adjacent to the museum of Marina Resort on the Cox's Bazar-Teknaf Marine Drive in Himchhari.

Fire service, lifeguards, and beach workers conducted a search until 7: 30 PM but couldn't find the two missing individuals.

According to police and lifeguard sources, a group of 12 people from Dhaka went to visit Himchhari beach.

Among them, five people went swimming in the sea. At that time, due to a large wave, all five got submerged. Later, lifeguards and locals rescued three of them. However, by then, they had already passed away. Searches are ongoing to find the other two missing individuals.

The three deceased tourists are Md Borhan (23), Saiful Islam (23), and Nafisul Haque (22) from Diabari, Uttara, Dhaka. Their bodies have been taken from Himchhari to the morgue at Cox's Bazar Sadar Hospital at night.

The the incident has been confirmed by the Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Ramu Police Station, AK Fazlul Haque. He told Prothom Alo that operations are ongoing to rescue the two missing individuals.

Imtiaz Ahmed, regional director of the private lifeguard company Sea-Safe, told Prothom Alo that the group of 12 tourists from Dhaka went to the beach adjacent to the museum of Marina Resort in Himchhari, about 9 kilometers south of the city, around 4 PM. Among them, five went swimming in the sea. When they got submerged due to waves, lifeguards and locals quickly initiated rescue efforts. Three were rescued but had already died.

Imtiaz Ahmed stated that from Kolatoli to Laboni Point along the Cox's Bazar sea beach, about five kilometers, Sea-Safe has 27 lifeguards available for rescue operations if someone goes missing while swimming.

However, there aren't enough personnel to conduct rescue operations along the vast stretch of beach from Kolatoli to the south, including Dariyanagar, Himchhari, Patuartek, Inani, and Teknaf.

Imtiaz Ahmed added that over 300,000 tourists are currently in Cox's Bazar. This afternoon, a large crowd gathered at Laboni Point for the immersion festival of idols. Seeing the crowd at various points on the beach, many people are rushing to swim at Dariyanagar and Himchhari beaches, which is increasing the risk of accidents.

According to Imtiaz Ahmed, at least 20 hidden channels have formed at Kolatoli, Sugandha, and Laboni Points, including Himchhari-Dariyanagar. Despite multiple places displaying red flags warning against swimming in dangerous areas, many are not adhering to the warnings.

Currently, more than 300, 000 tourists are staying in Cox''s Bazar. It has been reported by the concerned individuals that no rooms are available in any of the over 500 hotels, guesthouses, resorts, and cottages.
Most recently, on September 27 at Laboni Point on Cox''s Bazar beach, a tourist died from being swept away by the sea.

item.title: Rashid leads Afghanistan rout as Bangladesh crumble for 160
item.description:
Parvez Hossain scored a fighting 70, but Bangladesh were bowled out for 160 in 40 overs against Afghanistan in their must-win match of the tri-nation One Day International series at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday.

Leg-spinner Rashid Khan led Afghanistan’s bowling attack with four wickets for 31 runs, including two wickets in consecutive deliveries to wrap up Bangladesh’s innings.

Bangladesh, who elected to bat first, needed to beat Afghanistan by at least 41 runs to qualify for the final. Their hopes now depend on restricting Afghanistan to a sufficiently low total.

Bangladesh suffered an early collapse, losing four wickets for just 28 runs. Tanzid Hasan fell to Yamin Ahmadzai before Soumya Sarkar was bowled off the next ball, leaving the side in deep trouble.

Najmul Hossain offered some resistance with 15 off 23 balls but was caught behind, while captain Towhid Hridoy fell to Azmatullah Omarzai, who took a return catch.

With Bangladesh struggling at 28 for four in the seventh over, Parvez and Saif Hassan came together to rebuild the innings. The pair added 92 runs for the fifth wicket, helping Bangladesh cross 100 after 26 overs.

Parvez reached his half-century off 74 balls, scoring his second ODI fifty after being included in the squad for the tri-series as a replacement for Litton Das.

Saif, however, fell immediately after Parvez reached the milestone, attempting a big shot against Mohammad Nabi and offering a catch to Nangeyalia Kharote at midwicket. He scored 41 off 82 balls.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz lasted just seven deliveries before being caught at backward square leg off Bilal Sami for two.

Parvez continued to fight, bringing up Bangladesh’s 150 with a six off Nabi in the 39th over. But Rashid struck again, bowling Shoriful Islam for seven before trapping Parvez leg-before-wicket for 70 off 96 balls, an innings featuring five fours and two sixes.

Rashid then dismissed debutant Aliss Al Islam, caught by Nabi at slip, before Mustafizur Rahman was bowled first ball. Bangladesh lost their final three wickets in quick succession to finish on 160.
